questions.question_text: The active components of Khat produce pharmacological effects similar to which substance?
questions.explanation: Khat contains active alkaloids (cathine and cathinone) that produce stimulant effects similar to amphetamine, including increased alertness, energy, and euphoria, though with less potency.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman has completed detoxification for alcohol. She is interested in taking some medication to help her maintain abstinence. She is on tramadol for chronic back pain and has a history of ischaemic heart disease. Which of the following medications would be the best choice for this patient?
questions.explanation: Acamprosate is licensed for alcohol dependence and indicated for patients wanting to remain abstinent. Naltrexone and nalmefene are contraindicated with tramadol (opioid agonist). Disulfiram is contraindicated in coronary artery disease. Benzodiazepines are not indicated for relapse prevention.

questions.question_text: The half life of methadone in a individual with opioid dependence is
questions.explanation: Elimination of most synthetic opioids is complex. The peak plasma concentrations of oral methadone are reached within 2–6 hours, and initially plasma half-life is 4–6 hours in opioid-naive people and 24–36 hours after steady dosing of any type of opioid. It generally requires once- daily dosing. Methadone is highly protein bound and equilibrates widely throughout the body, which ensures little post-dosage variation in steady-state plasma concentrations. Methadone can be used for short-term detoxifi cation (7–30 days), long-term detoxifi cation (up to 180 days), and maintenance (treatment beyond 180 days) of opioid-dependent individuals. In contrast, the elimination of a sublingual dosage of buprenorphine occurs in two phases: an initial phase with a half-life of 3–5 hours and a terminal phase with a half-life of more than 24 hours. Buprenorphine dissociates from its receptor binding site slowly, which permits an every-other-day dosing schedule. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007; p. 1072.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which treatments for opioid dependence has been shown to reduce risk-taking behaviours linked to HIV transmission?
questions.explanation: Systematic reviews of methadone maintenance vs. non-opioid therapy conducted by the Cochrane collaboration shows that methadone has a superior retention rate than control conditions. Methadone maintenance treatment has also been shown to reduce risk behaviours (specifi cally reduction in needle sharing) and thereby has achieved a reduction in the transmission of HIV. Intake of illicit opioids decreased in the methadone maintenance group, as shown by fewer positive urine tests for ‘morphine’ in these groups. Although criminal activity was found to be less in the group that was on methadone maintenance, the statistics did not show a signifi cant difference. Nevertheless, individual randomized controlled trials have shown that methadone maintenance decreases criminal activity. In addition, methadone maintenance has shown to decrease rates of suicide and overdose in this population. Mattick RP, Breen C, Kimber J, et al. Methadone maintenance therapy versus no opioid replacement therapy for opioid dependence. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2003, Issue 2. Art. No.: CD002209.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which substances fulfills DSM5 diagnostic diagnostic requirements for the three major categories of use disorders, intoxication, and withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Cannabis fulfills the three major categories of substance use disorders. Tobacco has no clinically significant intoxication syndrome. Hallucinogens and inhalants lack consistent withdrawal syndromes. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., pp. 503– 540, 571– 577). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: A 40+ year old woman has completed detoxification for alcohol and wants a maintenance drug. She is on Tramadol for chronic back pain and has a history of ischemic heart disease. Which medication would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Acamprosate is safest in this scenario as naltrexone is contraindicated with opioids (tramadol), and disulfiram has cardiovascular risks in ischemic heart disease.

questions.question_text: In Alcoholics Anonymous, the therapeutic approach where patients acknowledge feeling helpless or powerless is part of which step?
questions.explanation: The First Step of the Twelve-Step Program requires participants to admit they are powerless over alcohol and that their lives have become unmanageable, establishing the foundation for recovery.

questions.question_text: A 34yearold male patient presents for an evaluation of substance use disorder. He works as a radiology technician at a major academic medical center. He reports escalating patterns of marijuana use over the past 4 months. He has been having difficulty with his memory, attention, and concentration, and this has negatively impacted his work performance. He avoids his family and spends much of his free time smoking marijuana. He has difficulty quitting because he becomes irritable when he does not use. He admits driving his car under the influence of marijuana. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of cannabisinduced mood disorder
A diagnosis of cannabis use disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of cannabis use disorder

questions.explanation: In this case the DSM5 criteria for cannabis use disorder are reflected by frequent use of marijuana in increasing quantities over a period of 4 months, continued use despite having psychological consequences (impaired cognition), recurrent use resulting in a failure to fulfill requirements at work, important family time given up for use, unsuccessful efforts to stop the use, withdrawal symptoms such as irritability, and use under physically hazardous situations such as driving a motor vehicle under the influence. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., pp. 509– 510). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: The supersensitivity model of substance use disorders in severely mentally ill patients proposes which mechanism?

options.text: Mental illness causes direct neurological damage predisposing to addiction
Genetic vulnerability predisposes to both conditions
Mentally ill patients are unusually sensitive to negative social and health consequences of substance exposure
Substance use directly initiates psychotic illness through kindling
Environmental factors alone explain both conditions

correct_answer.text: Mentally ill patients are unusually sensitive to negative social and health consequences of substance exposure

questions.explanation: The supersensitivity model proposes that mentally ill patients are unusually sensitive to negative social and health consequences of substance exposure, leading to a diagnosis of SUD. This differs from the common factor model (shared genetic vulnerability), the secondary illness model (substances cause mental illness), and the secondary use model (self-medication). The key distinction is heightened vulnerability to consequences rather than shared etiology.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man with schizophrenia uses alcohol heavily. His relative has a documented substance use disorder. Which model BEST explains why this patient might be vulnerable to both conditions?
questions.explanation: The common factor model is supported by the observation that patients with dual diagnosis have more relatives with substance use disorder, suggesting shared genetic or personality vulnerability. The presence of familial substance use disorder in this scenario supports common inherited factors rather than alcohol causing schizophrenia (secondary illness), self-medication of schizophrenia (secondary use), or heightened sensitivity to consequences (supersensitivity).

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is the best predictor of relapse to drinking in individuals with alcohol dependence?
questions.explanation: Difficulty falling asleep is the most replicated, subjective marker of relapse. Consistent with subjective reports, at least two studies found that polysomnographymeasured sleep onset latency (i.e., increased time to fall asleep) predicted drinking at at follow-up. One study with actigraphy-measured sleep onset latency also predicted similar outcomes.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which symptoms is NOT found in opiate withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Lacrimation – not dry eyes – is a symptom seen in opiate withdrawal. DSM-IV states that opiate withdrawal can be precipitated by cessation of (or reduction in) opioid use that has been heavy and prolonged (several weeks or longer) or administration of an opioid antagonist after a period of opioid use. Other symptoms typically associated with withdrawal are dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, rhinorrhoea, pupillary dilation, piloerection, sweating, diarrhoea, yawning, fever, and insomnia. Piloerection along with general ‘secretion’ from most of the glands is called the ‘cold turkey’, when people tend to detox without medical help. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 447.

questions.question_text: Mr Smith is presenting with a diagnosis of alcohol dependence syndrome. He receives an educational session regarding the effects of drinking and the potential benefi ts of abstinence. He does not make any immediate change in his attitude or behaviour but is prepared to consider altering his drinking habits. Which of the following phases of Prochaska’s transtheoretical model of change is he in?
questions.explanation: The stages of change model by Prochaska and DiClemente are stages that a person goes through when involved in a behavioural change. This may include a change in substance misuse behaviour, starting daily exercise, going on a diet, or changing a health-related behaviour, e.g. attempting to obtain a cervical smear. The fi rst stage is the precontemplation stage, where the person is not thinking of any imminent change and is happy the way things are. The second stage is contemplation, where he is considering a change in the near future. Preparation is when he gets ready or prepares to enforce the behavioural change. The action phase is when he implements the change, and in the maintenance phase he decides to continue the change in behaviour and attempts to prevent relapse. Thambirajah MS. Psychological Basis of Psychiatry. Elsevier, 2005, pp. 125–126.

questions.question_text: Chris and Ken are classmates at the local main school. Chris’s father has problems related to alcohol use, while Ken’s parents are teetotal. How many times is Chris more likely to develop an alcohol-related problem in later life than Ken, assuming other psychosocial factors are comparable?
questions.explanation: Alcohol use disorders run in families. A child with an alcoholic parent has a 4- to 10-fold increased risk of developing alcoholism themselves. This can be due to both genetic and environmental factors. Environmental infl uences include the availability of alcohol, parental attitudes, and peer pressure. Starting to drink before the age of 15 years is associated with a fourfold increased risk for lifetime alcoholism compared with starting at the age of 21 years. Severe childhood stressors, especially emotional, physical, and sexual abuse, are associated with up to seven times increased risk of alcoholism in adulthood. Childhood antisocial behaviour predicts regular alcohol use in early adolescence and the development of alcoholism later on. Enoch M. Genetic and environmental infl uences on the development of alcoholism: resilience vs. risk. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 2006; 1094: 193–201.

questions.question_text: Naloxone is mixed with buprenorphine because:

options.text: It reduces chances of misuse by deterring injection through precipitation of severe withdrawal

correct_answer.text: It reduces chances of misuse by deterring injection through precipitation of severe withdrawal

questions.explanation: Naloxone, an opioid antagonist, is combined with buprenorphine to deter intravenous misuse; if injected, naloxone precipitates severe acute withdrawal, making the combination unattractive for abuse.

questions.question_text: Cocaine's mechanism of action involves:

options.text: Direct blockade of the dopamine transporter

correct_answer.text: Direct blockade of the dopamine transporter

questions.explanation: Cocaine directly blocks the dopamine transporter (DAT), preventing dopamine reuptake and increasing dopaminergic neurotransmission.

questions.question_text: Which organ system or anatomical function is most commonly affected by chronic use of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA [Ecstasy])?
questions.explanation: There is significant evidence for long-term neurotoxic effects of MDMA use, including memory impairment, neuroendocrine function, sleep disturbance, psychological functioning, and serotonin system. Damage to brain microvasculature, white matter maturation, and axonal connections are included among neurotoxic events.

questions.question_text: A 45yearold female individual with alcoholic cirrhosis has abstained from drinking alcohol over the last month but continues to experience cravings. Her renal function is within the normal range. Which of the following medications would you recommend for her?
questions.explanation: Acamprosate is excreted by the kidneys and is not metabolized by the liver. It is preferred in patients with liver impairment. Liver disease should not affect its metabolism or blood level concentrations. ATed dISoRdeRS • 191 Re FeRe NCeS Work Group on Substance Use Disorders. (2006). questions.question_text: In the secondary illness model of substance use disorders in severely mentally ill patients, what mechanism is proposed?

options.text: Shared genetic vulnerability predisposes to both conditions
Substances lead to mental illness through a mechanism similar to kindling or behavioural sensitization
Patients self-medicate psychiatric symptoms with substances
Mental illness patients have increased sensitivity to the negative social and health consequences of substance use

correct_answer.text: Substances lead to mental illness through a mechanism similar to kindling or behavioural sensitization

questions.explanation: The secondary illness model posits that substance use disorder leads to mental illness by a mechanism similar to kindling or behavioural sensitization. This model proposes that repeated substance exposure progressively increases vulnerability to mental illness through neural sensitization. Evidence notess this model is popular with the lay public but differs from other models that propose different causal relationships.

questions.question_text: The frequency of suicide in those with substance abuse is second only to which of the following psychiatric disorders?
questions.explanation: Approximately ⅓ to ½ of those with opioid abuse or dependence and about 40% of those with alcohol abuse or dependence meet criteria for a major depressive disorder. Those with substance use alone are 20 times more likely to die by suicide than the general population... The frequency of suicide in substance use is only secondary to that in major depressive disorder.

questions.question_text: Tolerance and withdrawal were each considered valid criteria for the diagnosis of substance dependence in DSM-IV, although neither was required. which of the following options statements about tolerance and withdrawal in the DSM-5 diagnosis of substance use disorder is accurate?

options.text: Tolerance and withdrawal are no longer considered to be valid diagnostic symptoms of substance use disorder.
The definitions of tolerance and withdrawal have been updated because the previous definitions had poor interrater reliability.
The presence of either tolerance or withdrawal is now required to make a diagnosis of substance use disorder.
The presence of either tolerance or withdrawal is now required to make a substance use disorder diagnosis for some but not all classes of substances.

Both tolerance and withdrawal are still listed as possible criteria, but if they occur during appropriate medically supervised treatment, they may not be counted toward the diagnosis of a substance use disorder.

correct_answer.text: Both tolerance and withdrawal are still listed as possible criteria, but if they occur during appropriate medically supervised treatment, they may not be counted toward the diagnosis of a substance use disorder.

questions.explanation: In DSM-5, there is no change in how tolerance and withdrawal are defined, and either or both may be used to fulfill Criterion A for substance use disorder. Neither one is ever required, regardless of which substance is involved. Neither tolerance nor withdrawal may be counted toward a diagnosis when it occurs during appropriate medically supervised treatment (e.g., in a person taking opiates for pain, or stimulants for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder). A person receiving medically supervised treatment may still meet enough other criteria to be diagnosed with substance use disorder.

questions.question_text: Which symptoms characterize caffeine withdrawal according to DSM research criteria?

options.text: Headache, fatigue, drowsiness, anxiety, depression, and nausea

correct_answer.text: Headache, fatigue, drowsiness, anxiety, depression, and nausea

questions.explanation: Caffeine withdrawal symptoms include headache, marked fatigue or drowsiness, marked anxiety or depression, and nausea or vomiting, beginning within 12 hours, peaking at 24-48 hours, and lasting up to one week.

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes the mechanism of action of cocaine?
questions.explanation: Cocaine (and methylphenidate) directly blocks the dopamine transporter, preventing dopamine reuptake and increasing synaptic dopamine concentrations.

questions.question_text: Cue exposure therapy for substance use disorders involves

options.text: Administration of the substance in controlled doses
Exposure to drug cues without actual substance consumption to weaken conditioned responses
Cognitive restructuring of thoughts about drugs

correct_answer.text: Exposure to drug cues without actual substance consumption to weaken conditioned responses

questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy (CET) exposes patients to relevant drug cues (sight, smell of alcohol) without allowing consumption, attempting to weaken the conditioned stimulus-unconditioned stimulus link via extinction.

questions.question_text: A review examines withdrawal syndromes associated with various substances of abuse. Which substance does NOT produce a recognized withdrawal syndrome?
questions.explanation: LSD does not cause physical dependence or withdrawal syndrome.

questions.question_text: Thiamine deficiency in alcoholism develops through which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Multiple mechanisms including inadequate intake, reduced absorption, decreased hepatic storage, and impaired utilization

correct_answer.text: Multiple mechanisms including inadequate intake, reduced absorption, decreased hepatic storage, and impaired utilization

questions.explanation: Wernicke's encephalopathy is caused by thiamine deficiency through multiple mechanisms: inadequate dietary intake, reduced gastrointestinal absorption, decreased hepatic storage, and impaired utilization. No single mechanism alone explains all cases. The other options propose single mechanisms or incorrect physiologies not supported by the source.

questions.question_text: The classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, and nystagmus) is present in what percentage of patients?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that the classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and nystagmus is only present in 10% of patients. This low prevalence emphasizes why a high index of suspicion is needed, as WE rarely presents with all classical signs and symptoms. The other percentages represent distractors that do not match the stated epidemiological data.

questions.question_text: A 45yearold male individual receiving treatment in an addiction treatment program reports complete abstinence from alcohol use for 5 months. This has been confirmed by periodic urine toxicology screens and breathalyzers. He is attending Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and has a sponsor. He requests medication that will help mitigate his intermittent cravings. What would be the most appropriate pharmacological clinical measure for this individual?
questions.explanation: Acamprosate and disulfiram are FDAapproved drugs for alcohol use disorder. Acamprosate has the best evidence for the maintenance of complete abstinence from alcohol. ReFeReNCe Rosner, S., HacklHerrwerth, A., Leucht, S., et al. (2010). Acamprosate for alcohol dependence. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 9, CD004332.

questions.question_text: What is the primary mechanism of action of cocaine?
questions.explanation: Cocaine's rewarding effect is primarily mediated by blockade of the dopamine transporter (DAT), which increases dopamine concentration in limbic regions. D1 receptors are implicated in conditioned responses to cocaine, while D2 receptor occupancy contributes to its reinforcing effects.

questions.question_text: A 40yearold male patient presents for medically supervised detoxification in an inpatient addiction service. He has been using a number of substances prior to coming to the hospital. In the unit he is noted to have poor sleep and reports significant anxiety. He is very restless and has been pacing around the room. On physical examination he has tachycardia, with heart rate of 120 beats per minute, and sweaty palms and forehead. His hands exhibit a coarse tremor bilaterally. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this individual?
questions.explanation: Although anxiety, insomnia, and diaphoresis are nonspecific symptoms, coarse bilateral hand tremors are more specifically suggestive of alcohol withdrawal. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., pp. 499– 500, 506, 517– 518, 547– 548, 569– 570). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: Cue therapy is primarily used in the treatment of which condition?
questions.explanation: Cue therapy in addiction, also known as cue exposure therapy, is a type of psychological treatment used to help individuals with substance use disorders reduce their cravings and problematic behaviors related to substance abuse. This therapy focuses on identifying and managing the specific cues or triggers that lead to substance cravings and use.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which substances is most likely to be linked to polydrug use?
questions.explanation: Both adults and adolescents who use MDMA are more likely than those who use other drugs to be polydrug users and to have other substance use disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best characterizes the memory deficit during an alcoholic blackout?

options.text: Loss of all memories including remote memories and procedural skills
Anterograde amnesia with intact remote memory and ability to perform complex tasks, but inability to remember new information or how events occurred
Retrograde amnesia affecting only emotionally charged memories
Global amnesia similar to dementia with progressive worsening
Selective loss of verbal memory only, with preserved visual-spatial memory

correct_answer.text: Anterograde amnesia with intact remote memory and ability to perform complex tasks, but inability to remember new information or how events occurred

questions.explanation: Alcoholic blackouts are discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia where alcohol blocks new memory consolidation. During blackouts, remote memory remains intact and patients can perform complicated tasks, but they cannot remember these tasks or new information afterward. This specific short-term episodic memory deficit characterizes blackouts. The other options describe different amnestic syndromes or global cognitive impairment not consistent with blackouts.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach is particularly useful for alcohol addiction by managing triggers
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy (cue therapy) focuses on identifying and managing specific cues or triggers that lead to substance cravings and use. This approach is particularly effective in addiction treatment by helping individuals reduce responses to environmental triggers.

questions.question_text: Rate limiting enzyme in alcohol metabolism
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme in alcohol metabolism, catalyzing the conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde in the first step of alcohol breakdown.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which nonsubstancerelated disorders has been included in the substancerelated and addictive disorders chapter of DSM5?

options.text: A diagnosis of food addiction disorder
A diagnosis of shopping addiction disorder
A diagnosis of sex addiction disorder
A diagnosis of internet gambling disorder

questions.explanation: In addition to substancerelated disorders, the DSM5 chapter “SubstanceRelated and Addictive Disorders” also 6. du Sinha includes gambling disorder. There is evidence that gambling behavior activates the reward system similarly to the way it is activated by drugs of abuse. Other excessive behavioral patterns like Internet gambling have also been described, but evidencebased research examining these and other behavioral syndromes is limited. There is insufficient peerreviewed evidence to establish diagnosis of repetitive behavioral patterns such as food addiction, shopping addiction (sometimes called oniomania), or sex addiction. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., p. 481). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: Lifetime prevalence rates of alcohol use disorder is highest in

options.text: A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder

questions.explanation: Alcohol use disorder co-occurs with other major mental illnesses. The Epidemiology Catchment Area Study reported a 13.8% lifetime prevalence for alcohol abuse or dependence in persons with bipolar I disorder in the US general population. Lifetime prevalence of alcohol abuse or dependence are: bipolar I, 46.2%; bipolar II, 39.2%; schizophrenia, 33.7%; panic disorder, 28.7%; unipolar depression, 16.5%. Patients with mania had an odds ratio of 6.2 (highest) for co-occurring alcohol abuse and/or dependence. Considering the degree of psychiatric comorbidity among alcohol-dependent individuals, the National Comorbidity Survey showed that the odds ratio (OR) of having co-occurring lifetime diagnosis of mania in patients with a lifetime diagnosis of alcohol dependence was higher in both men (OR = 12.03) and women (OR = 5.3). Regier DA, Farmer ME, Rae DS, et al. Comorbidity of mental disorders with alcohol and other drug abuse. Results from the Epidemiologic Catchment Area (ECA) Study. Journal of the American Medical Association 1990; 264: 2511–2518. Kessler RC, Crum RM, Warner LA, et al. Lifetime co-occurrence of DSM-III-R alcohol abuse and dependence with other psychiatric disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey. Archives of General Psychiatry 1997; 54: 313–321. Fan AH FM, Masseling SJ, et al. Increased suicidality in mania complicated by alcoholism. Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 2007; 4: 34–39.

questions.question_text: Psychosocial interventions available for alcohol dependence include motivational enhancement treatment (MET), cognitive behavioural treatment (CBT) and 12-step facilitation programmes (TSF). Which of the following is NOT correct with regard to these interventions?

options.text: Four sessions of MET resulted in equivalent outcomes to 12 sessions of CBT
MET demonstrated greater cost-effectiveness than CBT
High levels of anger at baseline predicted better outcomes with CBT than MET
Individuals actively engaged in AA showed superior outcomes with TSF compared to MET
‘Meaning-seeking’ individuals fared better on TSF than MET

correct_answer.text: High levels of anger at baseline predicted better outcomes with CBT than MET

questions.explanation: This question can be answered using results from a study called Project MATCH (Matching Alcoholism Treatments to Client Heterogeneity). MATCH is one of the largest randomized trials to have examined psychosocial interventions for people with alcohol-related problems. The study is a multicentric study that involved randomizing over 1700 patients to MET, CBT, or TSF. This study demonstrated that four sessions of MET were as effective for treating alcohol dependence as 12 sessions of CBT or TSF therapy. The benefi ts from treatment persisted for up to 3 years. Clients with a higher degree of baseline anger fared better with MET than CBT or TSF. MET was found to be more cost-effective than CBT or TSF. The Project MATCH study and smaller patient-matching studies provide support for the effectiveness of TSF programmes. Patients in Project MATCH who received outpatient TSF were most likely to abstain from alcohol during the fi rst post-treatment year. TSF therapy led to a greater length of time before the patient’s fi rst relapse and to a higher percentage of abstinent patients at 1- and 3-year follow-up. Patients in Project MATCH with social networks supportive of not drinking responded better to TSF than MET, and that participation in AA was a mediator of this effect. Project MATCH found that patients who were rated high in ‘meaning-seeking’ fared better with TSF than CBT and MET at 1-year follow-up. Tyrer P and Silk KR. Cambridge Textbook of Effective Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. Cambridge University Press; 2008, p. 274.

questions.question_text: In therapy for substance dependence, admission of feeling helpless or powerless is characteristic of
questions.explanation: The 12-step model (used in AA and similar programs) involves acknowledging powerlessness over the substance and seeking higher power support, reflecting themes of helplessness.

questions.question_text: Which substance or class of substances in the Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders chapter of DSM-5 is not linked to a substance use disorder?
questions.explanation: Some caffeine users display symptoms consistent with problematic use, including tolerance and withdrawal. However, there are insufficient data to determine the clinical significance or prevalence of a caffeine use disorder.Therefore, caffeine use disorder does not appear in the Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders chapter of DSM-5 but instead is included as a proposed criteria set in the “Conditions for Further Study” chapter of DSM-5 Section III to encourage further research. In contrast, there is evidence that caffeine withdrawal and caffeine intoxication are clinically significant and sufficiently prevalent.

questions.question_text: In pathological intoxication, what is the typical duration before termination in sleep?
questions.explanation: That pathological intoxication may last for a few hours and terminate in prolonged sleep. This limited duration is a defining feature distinguishing it from other alcohol-related disorders. The other timeframes are either too brief or far too prolonged compared to the described few hours duration.

questions.question_text: What percentage of chronic alcoholics exhibited signs of Wernicke's encephalopathy in some case series?
questions.explanation: That in some case series, nearly one-eighth (12.5%) of all chronic alcoholics exhibited signs of Wernicke's encephalopathy. This high prevalence among heavy users underscores the importance of thiamine supplementation in this population. The other percentages do not match the stated epidemiological data.

questions.question_text: A 52-year-old man with alcohol dependence is admitted for detoxification. He last drank 6 hours ago. When would minor withdrawal symptoms typically begin?
questions.explanation: Minor alcohol withdrawal symptoms typically begin 4-12 hours after last drink.

questions.question_text: Alcoholic hallucinosis typically persists for which duration?
questions.explanation: That hallucinations in alcoholic hallucinosis usually last less than a week. The source further notes that hallucinations lasting more than 6 months should initiate suspicion of other psychoses such as schizophrenia, implying that persistence beyond this timeframe makes the diagnosis questionable. The other durations are either too short or contraindicate the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old man presents with bilateral conjunctival injection (red eyes), tachycardia (heart rate 108 bpm), mild hypotension (BP 102/65 mmHg), and palpitations. He appears anxious and reports feeling paranoid. There is a sweet smell on his clothing. Which substance is he most likely to have used?
questions.explanation: Red eyes, tachycardia, hypotension, paranoia, sweet smell—classic cannabis presentation.

questions.question_text: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step in alcohol metabolism?
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase catalyzes the first step of alcohol metabolism, converting ethanol to acetaldehyde. This is the rate-limiting step. Acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which converts acetaldehyde to acetyl-CoA, is not the rate-limiting step.

questions.question_text: What is the primary mechanism of action of psilocybin (magic mushroom)?

options.text: 5-HT2A agonism as a strong agonist, with moderate agonism at 5-HT1A and 5-HT2C

correct_answer.text: 5-HT2A agonism as a strong agonist, with moderate agonism at 5-HT1A and 5-HT2C

questions.explanation: Psilocybin is a strong agonist at 5-HT2A and a moderate agonist at 5-HT1A and 5-HT2C receptors, with these serotonergic pathways being the common mechanism of action shared across hallucinogens.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes lofexidine?
questions.explanation: In opioid detoxification, if short duration of treatment is desirable, a2 adrenergic agonists such as lofexidine and clonidine are preferred to methadone.

questions.question_text: Acamprosate is a
questions.explanation: Acamprosate is a synthetic taurine analogue, which appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter systems, although the mechanism has not been fully established.

questions.question_text: Which is a form of negative reinforcement used in the treatment of alcohol dependence?
questions.explanation: The use of disulfiram - a deterrent agent (also called alcohol-sensitizing drug) - is a form of behavioural modification with negative reinforcement used in the treatment of alcohol dependence.

questions.question_text: A mother wants to know the likelihood that her teenage son who has been smoking cannabis for 6 months will develop schizophrenia. The correct answer is
questions.explanation: At present, there is a consensus that cannabis increases the risk of psychosis 2-3 times, especially if the exposure started early in adolescence and persisted to adulthood.

questions.question_text: The term that refers to the neglect of all leisure and other alternate forms of pleasure apart from alcohol is
questions.explanation: Salience refers to the neglect of all leisure and other alternate form of pleasures apart from alcohol. One's life revolves around getting alcohol, storing it, saving money to buy it, making opportunities to drink, etc. Narrowing of repertoire: A social drinker may drink in various situations at various places and may have various drinks of his choice. A dependent drinker will settle into a fixed setting, sticking to one beverage. This may help him maintain a steady level of alcohol in the blood without much fluctuation. Note that some widening of repertoire is inevitable in the career of an alcohol drinker - moving from weekends only to all days of the week, etc.

questions.question_text: Choose the one feature which is not defined under Edwards and Gross criteria (1976) for alcohol dependence syndrome.
questions.explanation: Edwards and Gross criteria (1976) for alcohol dependence: 1. narrowed repertoire 2. salience of alcohol seeking behaviour 3. increased tolerance 4. repeated withdrawals 5. Drinking to prevent or relieve withdrawals. 6. subjective awareness of compulsion 7. reinstatement after abstinence

questions.question_text: A 49-year-old man is highly alcohol dependent. Due to various physical problems he was strongly advised to abstain. Unfortunately since last episode of intoxication he has developed recurrent voices that frighten him. In spite of 2 months of abstinence these hallucinations continue, and he now presents with persecutory delusions. Which of the following diagnosis best suits his presentation?
questions.explanation: The DSM has a diagnostic criteria for alcohol-induced psychotic disorders (popularly called alcoholic hallucinosis) and further allows the specification of onset (during intoxication or withdrawal). The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign and threatening. The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the hallucinations though afterwards they may realise the untrue nature.

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old boy who has used cannabis for the first time complains that his legs are being pulled and moved. Which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Kinaesthetic hallucinations and passivity can occur under the acute intoxication-related effects of cannabis.

questions.question_text: Which term refers to 'discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication'?
questions.explanation: Alcoholic blackouts: Alcohol-related blackouts are not included in DSM-IV/ ICD10. Blackouts are discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication. During a blackout (at the time of intoxication), remote memory is intact but patients experience specific short-term episodic memory deficit (they can talk about their childhood etc., but cannot remember what topic the conversation is about or how did they come to where they were) They can even perform complicated tasks but later will not remember these. The memory gap usually lasts for hours, rarely a day or more. Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories the at the hippocampus.

questions.question_text: Characteristic features of delirium tremens include all except
questions.explanation: Features of alcohol withdrawal: Usually starts within 12 hours of the last drink. Tremor, diaphoresis, sleeplessness, GI distress and anxiety are prominent. Increased urge and craving for alcohol may be seen. The severity of symptoms depends on the degree of pre-existent drinking. If unattended, symptoms may peak in 48 hours. In these cases, seizures may occur. These are grand-mal seizures especially common in those who had previous seizures (epilepsy or withdrawal seizures), head injury and electrolyte imbalance such as hyponatraemia or hypokalaemia. In around 5% patients, delirium tremens may set in with disturbed autonomic functions (pulse, temperature and blood pressure changes on either direction), clouded consciousness, hallucinations (often Lilliputian) and agitation.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum duration required to make a diagnosis of alcohol dependence according to ICD-10 criteria?
questions.explanation: ICD10 alcohol dependence requires at least 3 features out of following list satisfied in the last 12 months: 1. intense desire to drink alcohol 2. difficulty in controlling the onset, termination and the level of drinking 3. experiencing withdrawal symptoms if alcohol is not taken 4. use of alcohol to relieve from withdrawal symptoms 5. tolerance as evidenced by the need to escalate dose over time to achieve same effect 6. salience - neglecting alternate forms of leisure or pleasure in life 7. A narrowing personal repertoire of alcohol use.

questions.question_text: A patient with long-standing anxiety being managed by GP was recently seen by her psychiatrist who made changes in her medications. She presents to the A and E with hallucinations of her joints being moved and nausea with agitation and anxiety. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Symptoms of benzodiazepine withdrawal include autonomic hyperactivity, increased tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations or illusions,psychomotor agitation and anxiety. Sometimes grand mal seizures can occur. Kinaesthetic hallucinations are characteristically related to benzodiazepine withdrawal and have been reported in some patients. Alcoholism in the Elderly - American Family Physician, http://www.aafp.org/afp/20 /p1710.html (accessed April 10, 2015).

questions.explanation: According to DSM, caffeinism is defined as recent consumption of caffeine usually in excess of 250 MG accompanied by five or more of the following; restlessness

questions.question_text: Flashback phenomenon is commonly reported after ingesting which of the following substances?
questions.explanation: Descriptive Psychopathology Long after ingesting a hallucinogen like LSD; a person can experience a flashback of hallucinogenic symptoms. This syndrome is diagnosed as hallucinogen persisting perception disorder in DSM-5. This reexperiencing of perceptual symptoms following cessation of hallucinogen use is characterised by seeing geometric hallucinations, false perceptions of movement in the peripheral visual fields, flashes or intensified colours, trails of images of moving objects, positive afterimages, halos around objects, macropsia, and micropsia. This is also called flashback phenomenon. The following can trigger a flashback: Emotional stress, Sensory deprivation, Use of another psychoactive substance, such as alcohol or marijuana. (Excerpts from Kaplan & Sadock Synopsis of Psychiatry 10th ed)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?

options.text: Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium.
These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time.
The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.
The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the
hallucinations though afterwards they may realise the untrue nature.

correct_answer.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

questions.explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis: The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign and threatening. The hallucinations usually last only for few days, during which the patients lack insight and believe in an external source for hallucinations though afterwards they often realise their untrue nature. These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time. Delusions are usually secondary interpretations of the hallucinations. The patient is usually distressed, anxious, and restless. Unlike those experiencing delirium tremens, those with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium. As an 26/73 empirical timescale, hallucinations lasting for more than six months should initiate suspicion of other Descriptive Psychopathology psychoses including schizophrenia. The hallucinations respond well and rapidly to antipsychotics. The prognosis is good provided that the person remains abstinent. But the evidence base for treating alcoholic hallucinosis is very poor.

questions.question_text: Mr. Collins is a 48-year-old man with a diagnosis of alcohol dependence. He previously had 10 years of abstinence after treatment with disulfiram but relapsed 3 years ago. He is keen to have disulfiram again. Which of the following is a side-effect of disulfiram in the absence of alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram works by inhibiting the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which means that many of the effects of a hangover are felt immediately after alcohol is consumed. This produces numerous adverse side-effects, including: flushing, throbbing in head and neck, throbbing headache, respiratory difficulty, nausea, copious vomiting, sweating, thirst, chest pain, palpitation, dyspnoea, hyperventilation, tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, marked uneasiness, weakness, vertigo, blurred vision, and confusion. In severe reactions there may be respiratory depression, cardiovascular collapse, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, acute congestive heart failure, unconsciousness, convulsions, and death. In the absence of alcohol, the most common side-effects are headache and a metallic or garlic-like taste in the mouth. Less commonly, patients can experience a reduction in libido, liver problems, skin rash, and nerve inflammation.

questions.question_text: Miss Clarke is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of opiate dependence syndrome who is under a substance misuse service. She attends clinic and sees you to request that you prescribe her an alpha-2-agonist medication to prevent her experiencing withdrawals whilst she stops using opiates. She has a history of experiencing marked hypotension in the past. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate for Miss Clarke?
questions.explanation: Both Clonidine and Lofexidine are used to reduce the withdrawal symptoms associated with stopping opiates. Clonidine is commonly associated with hypotension, whilst this is not seen with lofexidine with the same frequency. Interesting, clonidine can be used in some patients with profound and persistent hypotension due to it having a limited central hypotensive effect in these patients.

questions.question_text: Miss Davies is a 28-year-old woman with a diagnosis of opiate dependence. She is keen to become abstinent and asks if there is any medication she could take that would counteract the effect of opioids and help her stop their use. Which of the following is a medication that would best fit this description?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist, which can be used in patients with opiate dependence. Naloxone is also an opioid antagonist but is short-acting and not useful in maintaining abstinence. Methadone is a replacement therapy for opiates and does not have any antagonism for them. Clonidine is used to manage opiate withdrawals. Baclofen is currently being investigated for potential use in alcohol dependence.

questions.question_text: In the neurobiology of alcohol addiction, from where is the initial release of dopamine?
questions.explanation: The ventral-tegmental area (VTA) is one of the components of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway. The neurones (cell bodies located in the VTA) stretch to the nucleus accumbens (NA). The VTA neurones release dopamine which acts on neurones in the NA, an area of the brain associated with motivation, reward and reinforcement learning. (Ref: Clapp, P., Bhave, S. V., & Hoffman, P. L. (2008). How Adaptation of the Brain to Alcohol Leads to Dependence: A Pharmacological Perspective. Alcohol Reasearch & Health, 31(4), 310- 339).

questions.question_text: Mr. Stevens is a 24-year-old man with a diagnosis of amphetamine misuse. Which of the following parts of the brain is most directly affected by amphetamine use?
questions.explanation: Amphetamine use is associated with changes to the dopaminergic neurons in the striatum, particularly in the caudate and putamen.
